I've been working this land for forty years. I know every corner of it. My main job is to keep the family fed and make enough to cover expenses and save a little. I don't gamble with untested methods — I do what has worked, season after season.

My wheat-maize rotation is the backbone. That gives me 18 mu of reliable income and food. After wheat comes off in June, I need to decide what goes back in. Maize on most of it — 15 mu — because the price is steady and my equipment is set up for it. On the remaining 3 mu of those wheat fields I'll rotate in mungbean (2 mu) and soybean (1 mu) to break the disease cycle a bit and sell at the local market. My wife manages the household account and she likes having those for cash.

Cotton I keep at 4 mu. It's hard work, especially picking in September, but my wife and I handle it and the price has been acceptable. I won't expand it because my back is not what it used to be.

Chrysanthemum I keep at 4 mu. I grow the medicinal variety. The buyers come to the village in October. It needs careful watering and pest watch but the price per jin makes it worth it.

Spinach fills the remaining 2.1 mu. I sow it in late August and harvest in October-November. It sells fresh quickly at the county market and takes little input.

For seeds, I use hybrid varieties for wheat and maize — the county agricultural station sells them and I've used Jimai series wheat and Zhengdan 958 maize for years. For chrysanthemum I use cuttings from my own stock, same traditional variety my father grew. Cotton I use Bt hybrid seed to cut down on bollworm spraying.

Fertilizer I apply based on what I've always done. Compound fertilizer at planting, urea top-dressed later. I water from my well — 4 irrigations for wheat (pre-winter, jointing, heading, and one before harvest if it's dry), 3 for maize, more for cotton and chrysanthemum because those need steady moisture in summer.
